chapter_theme: Neythal: on the sea shore the heroine grieves the shore lord's absence and coldness, turning to the sea, the heron, the stork and the anril as fellow sufferers, witnesses or messengers (57, 60, 62-66), presses through her friend for marriage as her mother grows suspicious (58), waits for his chariot (59), is overwhelmed at the sight of him (67), and the friend reassures her of his love (61) and reproaches him with the paired crab (68).

57.reading: The speaker says that the heart which has come to know the shore lord, of the bank where the roaming cold wind lifts the down of the white herons ranged along it, for a simple fool is itself a sweet thing, for is not the truth a gain to one's life?
57.nuance: The down that the wind picks up and carries off is the lightest thing on the shore, and the poem sets it beside a man the heart now judges light; only one correspondence can be named, so it is scene, not ullurai. The bitterness is turned into consolation: knowing the truth, however hard, is a gain.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore lord and the herons of the bank

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the speaker is taken to be the heroine, disillusioned with the man, and no addressee is named

58.reading: The heroine asks her friend what is to be done, since there is no kindness even in his eyes and her mother's face has turned the same way, and bids her tell the lord of the shore grove of golden-flowered punnai whether this is fitting, saying she has no one but him.
58.nuance: The mother's face has 'become that too' (அதுவாகும்): the secret is close to discovery at home just as the lover cools, so the plea that she has none but him is a push toward marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: the punnai grove of the sea shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; தோழி in line 1 names the addressee, and the message is for the hero

59.reading: Taking the noise of birds for the bells of the swift horses of the shore lord, of the wide grove with its heaped sand dunes, the girl of the curved earrings rose and then turned back when she heard what it was, afraid that the people of the little hamlet would make talk of her.
59.nuance: Her turning back has two causes folded together: the sound was only birds, and going out to meet a chariot would give the hamlet its gossip; the waiting girl is caught between longing and the town's eyes.

thinai_evidence.note: the sand dunes and grove of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the heroine is spoken of in the third person (பெயர்ந்தாள்), so the friend is taken to report her waiting to the hero

60.reading: The heroine asks whether it is because the lord of the dark backwater of sapphire-blue neythal took his fill of her beauty and left that the sea, like her, does not sleep as its tide shifts over the packed sand dunes.
60.nuance: She does not say the sea keeps her awake; she makes the sea a fellow sufferer and gives it her own cause, so the restless tide becomes a second heroine deserted by the same man.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower and the sea

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; she speaks to herself of the sea

61.reading: The friend tells the jewelled girl that the cool lord of the curved backwater, fragrant with neythal that meets the eye, is no longer his own master: holding it manliness to have been caught by her lovely smile, he comes on his well-made chariot.
61.nuance: கண்ணுறு நெய்தல் can be the neythal that meets the eye or the neythal like eyes; and the joke is that his manliness consists in being captured, so the friend reassures the girl by mocking him gently.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal of the curved backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; ஆயிழாய் in line 2 names the addressee

62.reading: The heroine asks whether the heron living in the shore grove does not know the cruelty of the lord of the shore, whose leaping waves strike the shoals of sharks till their kinds are mixed, though it saw him go off to the forest land and turn graceless.
62.nuance: The heron was the one witness of the secret union, and her question accuses it of keeping silent; the waves that throw the sharks into confusion carry the cruelty she names, but only one correspondence is stated, so it is not ullurai.

thinai_evidence.note: the heron of the shore grove and the shore lord

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; she speaks of the heron that saw the secret union

63.reading: The heroine asks her friend whether merely seeing with their eyes the lord of the shore, where the many fish the fishermen brought in their fine-corded nets are snatched as they dry, will be enough, and proposes that they accost him and say 'give back her colour'.
63.nuance: The catch the fishermen laboured for is snatched while it dries, as her colour, won from her, was taken; only this one correspondence holds, so it stays scene, a near miss on ullurai condition 3.

thinai_evidence.note: the fishermen and their drying catch

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; என்தோழி in line 3 names the addressee

64.reading: The heroine tells the red-feathered stork that holds small fish in its cheek and lives only for its young, with its soft breaking cry, that it knows the path by which the lord of the dark backwater of winding water went away, it, the killer of fish.
64.nuance: மீன்தபு நீ turns the praise into reproach: the devoted parent is also a killer, as the man who seemed gentle proved cruel.

thinai_evidence.note: the stork of the dark backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; she addresses the stork

iraicchi.act: the stork carries small fish in its cheek and gives itself wholly to its young
iraicchi.sense: a bird that keeps faith with its own brood has seen the road of a man who did not keep faith with his

65.reading: The heroine bids the curve-beaked anril, which eats the food it wants in the clear-watered dark backwater and roosts joined with its mate on the palmyra, to accost the cool lord of the shore and say in tender words 'give back her colour'.
65.nuance: மடமொழி may be the tender words she lends the bird or a vocative to a soft-spoken friend; the vocative mark on the anril in line 2 favours the first.

thinai_evidence.note: the anril on the palmyra of the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; she addresses the anril

iraicchi.act: the anril feeds and roosts on the palmyra always joined with its mate
iraicchi.sense: the bird that never parts from its mate is the fitting voice to shame the man who parted from her

66.reading: Having made sure that the lord of the curved backwater, where crabs walk the dunes overgrown with adumbu creeper, will show no grace, the speaker asks whether that thief-hearted man will go off by another's path, walking away while her good bangles slip.
66.nuance: Who 'makes sure' (தெளிந்து) is open: the girl, who has learnt he will not be kind, or the man, sure of his own coldness; அயல்நெறி may be another woman's way or simply a road away from her.

thinai_evidence.note: the crab and the adumbu dunes of the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; the speaker is taken to be the friend, speaking of the man and the girl in the third person

67.reading: The heroine says that she, left standing bereft of her senses, became certain she had seen the lord of the shore, where ships laden with goods ply the great sea that yields clustered pearls, in the grove of mundakam.
67.nuance: The certainty comes only after the sight, because the sight itself took her senses away; the pearl-yielding, trading sea sets him among wealth beyond her own shore.

thinai_evidence.note: pearls of the sea and the mundakam grove

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; no addressee is named, and the friend is the likely hearer

68.reading: The friend tells the lord of the matchless dark backwater, where the forked-legged crab stays with its mate on the dune of sand the climbing waves have left, that her friend's shoulders have become overspread with pallor.
68.nuance: The crab's line has no verb of its own (தனபெடை யோடு): it is simply with its mate, and the friend leaves the man to finish the thought.

thinai_evidence.note: the crab of the dune and the dark backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon gives no thurai; சேர்ப்ப! and என்தோழி in line 3 give speaker and addressee

iraicchi.act: the crab keeps with its mate on the dune when the waves draw back
iraicchi.sense: even the crab stays beside its mate, yet he leaves her friend to pale

links.note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 50: the heroine says she rose at what she took for his horses' bells and turned back on hearing it was birds. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 59 tells the same mistake of her in the third person, with the same words புள்ளரவம் கேட்டுப் பெயர்ந்.
links.teaches: The two venbas share a stock scene, and the second adds what the first leaves out: in the heroine's own telling she turns back from a melting heart, in the onlooker's telling from fear of the hamlet's talk, so the formula carried either the private grief or the public danger of kalavu waiting.

links.note: Natrinai 335: the sea's sound never stops and the tide comes and goes, and with the anril and the lute the night cannot be survived. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 60: the sea, like her, does not sleep as the tide shifts, because the shore lord took her beauty and left.
links.teaches: In the Natrinai the restless sea is one of the things that keep the heroine awake, while the venba makes the same tide sleepless for her own reason, so the pair shows the neythal sea turning from a cause of sleeplessness into a fellow sufferer.

links.note: Kuruntokai 25: no one was there but the thief, only a heron watching for aaral fish on the day he took her. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: does the heron of the grove not know his cruelty, though it saw him go and turn graceless?
links.teaches: Kuruntokai's heron proves that the secret union had no witness worth the name, and the venba goes one step on, upbraiding that same silent witness for not knowing what it saw, so the heron of kalavu moves from absent proof to complicit bystander.

links.note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 45: will the herons of the grove let his oath go unpunished? Ainthinai Ezhupathu 62: the heron of the grove saw his cruelty and does not know it. On a plain reading one makes the herons guarantors of his oath and the other finds the heron a useless witness.
links.teaches: Held together, the two shore venbas show the heroine's trust in the grove's herons as witnesses of a secret oath collapsing once he has gone: the birds she counted on to hold him are the birds she then reproaches for seeing nothing.

links.note: Kuruntokai 236: the friend tells the shore lord to go if he must, but first give back the beauty he consumed (நீ உண்டவென் னலனே). Ainthinai Ezhupathu 63: the heroine would accost him herself and say 'give back the colour' (வண்ணந்தா).
links.teaches: The demand to give back consumed beauty belongs to the friend in Kuruntokai, but the venba puts it in the heroine's own mouth and doubts that only looking at him would suffice, so the pair shows the reproach moving from the go-between to the injured woman herself.

links.note: Both poems end on the same demand, வண்ணம் தா ... தொடுத்து: in 63 the heroine and her friend would accost the shore lord themselves; in 65 she sends the paired anril to say it.
links.teaches: Two poems of one sequence ending on the same words show the demand for her colour passing from a plan to face him to a message given to a bird, which tells us how far her confidence in meeting him has fallen.

links.note: Ainthinai Aimpathu 42: the heroine begs the crab not to blur the tracks of his chariot so she can gaze at the path he took. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 64: she tells the stork that it knows the path by which he went.
links.teaches: In both venbas the path of the departed shore lord is known only to the shore's creatures, the crab who can erase it and the stork who has seen it, so the pair shows the neythal heroine's knowledge of his leaving lodged entirely in what the animals of the beach can keep or destroy.

links.note: Akananuru 170: since grove, backwater and punnai will not speak, the woman begs the crab to carry her word to the shore lord, at midnight when the sea-crow dreams beside its mate. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 65: she bids the anril, joined with its mate, to tell him 'give back the colour'.
links.teaches: The long poem shows why a creature is her messenger, since the land itself is mute, while the venba chooses a messenger whose own paired life is the reproach, so together they show the creature-messenger used first for its reach and then for its example.

links.note: Kural 1157: do not the bangles slipping from my wrist spread the news that the shore lord has left me? Ainthinai Ezhupathu 66: will the thief-hearted shore lord walk off by another path while her good bangles slip?
links.teaches: The couplet makes the slipping bangle a herald announcing his departure, while the venba places it at the moment of his going and calls his heart a thief's, so the pair qualifies the Kural's sign: the bangle that tells the town of his leaving also convicts him of planned deceit.

links.note: Akananuru 380: the shore lord, wooing, showed the girls a crab carrying a naaval fruit to its mate in its burrow and said 'this is a fine way'. Ainthinai Ezhupathu 68: the friend tells the shore lord of the crab with its mate on the dune, and that her friend has paled.
links.teaches: In the Akananuru the hero himself offers the crab that cares for its mate as a sign of how he will behave, and in the venba the friend returns the same crab to him as a reproach while the girl pales, so the pair shows a courting pledge turned into the evidence against the man who gave it.

source_issues: Verses 57 (இனி(து)), 58 (நின்னல்ல(து), இல்லென்(று)), 65 (துறைவற்(கு)) and 68 (நீக்கியிட்(டு)) print editorial brackets that restore elided letters; the restored readings were used.
Verse 62 line 2 reads ஏறிதிரைச் where the sense needs எறிதிரைச் (leaping waves); and the line break splits கொடுமை யறியாகொல் with a dash.
Verse 68 line 2 reads தனபெடை, likely தன் பெடை, and the clause of the crab has no finite verb; the sense 'with its mate' was taken.
